'''陸奥総社宮'''（むつそうしゃのみや）は、[[宮城県]][[多賀城市]]市川字奏社にある[[神社]]である。[[陸奥国]]31[[郡]]の100社の[[祭神]]を祀る。
==歴史== 一千年程前に陸奥[[国府]][[多賀城]]に赴任した[[国司]]が国内の神社を参拝するために、多賀城の近くに合祀勧請したのが始まり。 多賀城の廃絶後も残り、[[江戸時代]]には[[仙台藩 |仙台藩主]][[伊達氏]]を始め世間一般から篤い信仰を受けた。 現在も安産守護、海上守護、歳徳、武徳、大難除けの神として崇敬されている。
== 交通 == [[東日本旅客鉄道|JR東日本]][[東北本線]][[国府多賀城駅]]より徒歩30分
== 関連項目 == * [[多賀城]]
==外部リンク== *[http://www5e.biglobe.ne.jp/~ALLURE/mutu-sosya-page1.html 陸奥総社宮]
{{DEFAULTSORT:むつそうしゃのみや}} [[Category:宮城県の神社]] [[Category:多賀城市]] {{shinto-stub}}

鳥居の後ろ、雨覆いの掛けられた白壁には陸奥国100社の名前が書かれている。]] '''陸奥総社宮'''（むつそうしゃのみや）は、[[宮城県]][[多賀城市]]市川字奏社にある[[神社]]である。[[陸奥国]]の[[総社]]で、陸奥国内31[[郡]]の100社の[[祭神]]を祀る。旧社格は[[村社]]。 ==歴史== [[中世#日本|中世]]の[[律令制]]において[[国司]]は任国内の諸社に神拝する事が定められていたが、国内の神社を一箇所に集め、そこを詣でることで巡拝の手間を省くことが広まった。陸奥[[国府]][[多賀城]]に赴任した[[国司]]が広大な国内の巡拝を一箇所で行うため、多賀城東門の近くに合祀勧請したのが当社の始まりとされる。 多賀城の廃絶後も残り、[[鎌倉時代]]には陸奥留守職に任じられ、「留守」姓を名乗るようになった伊沢氏により崇敬を受け、祭祀料として3,000刈の社地が寄進された。[[江戸時代]]になると[[仙台藩]][[伊達政宗|初代藩主正宗]]による領内寺社整備が行われ、[[鹽竈神社]][[別当]]の[[法蓮寺 (塩竈市)|法蓮寺]]末寺、市川山神奏院が別当として置かれ社務が行われた。『宮城県神社名鑑』宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年1月　より。によれば、歴代藩主の尊崇篤く、親拝代参などがあったとされる。また、世間一般からも篤い信仰を受けた。 [[明治]]4年（[[1871年]]）10月に村社に列格。明治41年（[[1908年]]）に貴船神社ほか7社を合併し、[[大正]]12年（[[1923年]]）8月には[[近代社格制度#諸社|供進社]]に指定された。 現在も安産守護、海上守護、歳徳、武徳、大難除けの神として崇敬されている。 == 交通 == [[東日本旅客鉄道|JR東日本]][[東北本線]][[国府多賀城駅]]より徒歩30分 == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == *宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年10月 == 関連項目 == * [[多賀城]] ==外部リンク== *[http://www5e.biglobe.ne.jp/~ALLURE/mutu-sosya-page1.html 陸奥総社宮] {{Commons|Category:Mutsusoushanomiya}} {{DEFAULTSORT:むつそうしゃのみや}} [[Category:宮城県の神社]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:多賀城市]] {{shinto-stub}}

鳥居の後ろ、雨覆いの掛けられた白壁には陸奥国100社の名前が書かれている。]] '''陸奥総社宮'''（むつそうしゃのみや）は、[[宮城県]][[多賀城市]]市川字奏社にある[[神社]]である。[[陸奥国]]の[[総社]]で、陸奥国内31[[郡]]の100社の[[祭神]]を祀る。旧社格は[[村社]]。 ==歴史== [[中世#日本|中世]]の[[律令制]]において[[国司]]は任国内の諸社に神拝する事が定められていたが、国内の神社を一箇所に集め、そこを詣でることで巡拝の手間を省くことが広まった。陸奥[[国府]][[多賀城]]に赴任した[[国司]]が広大な国内の巡拝を一箇所で行うため、多賀城東門の近くに合祀勧請したのが当社の始まりとされる。 多賀城の廃絶後も残り、[[鎌倉時代]]には陸奥留守職に任じられ、「留守」姓を名乗るようになった伊沢氏により崇敬を受け、祭祀料として3,000刈の社地が寄進された。[[江戸時代]]になると[[仙台藩]][[伊達政宗|初代藩主政宗]]による領内寺社整備が行われ、[[鹽竈神社]][[別当]]の[[法蓮寺 (塩竈市)|法蓮寺]]末寺、市川山神奏院が別当として置かれ社務が行われた。『宮城県神社名鑑』宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年1月　より。によれば、歴代藩主の尊崇篤く、親拝代参などがあったとされる。また、世間一般からも篤い信仰を受けた。 [[明治]]4年（[[1871年]]）10月に村社に列格。明治41年（[[1908年]]）に貴船神社ほか7社を合併し、[[大正]]12年（[[1923年]]）8月には[[近代社格制度#諸社|供進社]]に指定された。 現在も安産守護、海上守護、歳徳、武徳、大難除けの神として崇敬されている。 == 交通 == [[東日本旅客鉄道|JR東日本]][[東北本線]][[国府多賀城駅]]より徒歩30分 == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == *宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年10月 == 関連項目 == * [[多賀城]] ==外部リンク== *[http://mutsusousya.web.fc2.com/index.html 陸奥総社宮] *[http://k2.fc2.com/cgi-bin/hp.cgi/mutsusousya/ 携帯版 陸奥総社宮] {{Commons|Category:Mutsusoushanomiya}} {{DEFAULTSORT:むつそうしゃのみや}} [[Category:宮城県の神社]] [[Category:村社]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:多賀城市]] {{shinto-stub}}

鳥居の後ろ、雨覆いの掛けられた白壁には陸奥国100社の名前が書かれている。]] '''陸奥総社宮'''（むつそうしゃのみや）は、[[宮城県]][[多賀城市]]市川字奏社にある[[神社]]である。[[陸奥国]]の[[総社]]で、陸奥国内31[[郡]]の100社の[[祭神]]を祀る。[[近代社格制度|旧社格]]は村社。 ==歴史== [[中世#日本|中世]]の[[律令制]]において[[国司]]は任国内の諸社に神拝する事が定められていたが、国内の神社を一箇所に集め、そこを詣でることで巡拝の手間を省くことが広まった。陸奥[[国府]][[多賀城]]に赴任した[[国司]]が広大な国内の巡拝を一箇所で行うため、多賀城東門の近くに合祀勧請したのが当社の始まりとされる。 多賀城の廃絶後も残り、[[鎌倉時代]]には陸奥留守職に任じられ、「留守」姓を名乗るようになった伊沢氏により崇敬を受け、祭祀料として3,000刈の社地が寄進された。[[江戸時代]]になると[[仙台藩]][[伊達政宗|初代藩主政宗]]による領内寺社整備が行われ、[[鹽竈神社]][[別当]]の[[法蓮寺 (塩竈市)|法蓮寺]]末寺、市川山神奏院が別当として置かれ社務が行われた。『宮城県神社名鑑』宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年1月　より。によれば、歴代藩主の尊崇篤く、親拝代参などがあったとされる。また、世間一般からも篤い信仰を受けた。 [[明治]]4年（[[1871年]]）10月に村社に列格。明治41年（[[1908年]]）に貴船神社ほか7社を合併し、[[大正]]12年（[[1923年]]）8月には[[近代社格制度#諸社|供進社]]に指定された。 現在も安産守護、海上守護、歳徳、武徳、大難除けの神として崇敬されている。 == 保存樹木 == 多賀城市の保存樹木が2本ある『多賀城市史』第1巻27頁。以下の樹齢等の数値も同じ。。 *陸奥総社宮の白木蓮 - [[ハクモクレン]] - 1985年調査での推定樹齢約220年（江戸時代）、樹高16.8メートル、周囲2.2メートル。 *陸奥総社宮の老杉 - [[スギ]]。1985年調査での推定樹齢約600年（室町時代）、樹高25.6メートル、周囲4.88メートル。神社の神木で、正月に[[注連縄|しめ縄]]をかける。 == 交通 == [[東日本旅客鉄道|JR]][[東北本線]] [[国府多賀城駅]]より徒歩30分 == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == *多賀城市史編纂委員会 編 『多賀城市史』第1巻（原始・古代・中世）、多賀城市、1997年。 *宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年10月 == 関連項目 == * [[多賀城]] ==外部リンク== *[http://mutsusousya.web.fc2.com/index.html 陸奥総社宮] *[http://k2.fc2.com/cgi-bin/hp.cgi/mutsusousya/ 携帯版 陸奥総社宮] {{Commons|Category:Mutsusoushanomiya}} {{shinto-stub}} {{DEFAULTSORT:むつそうしやのみや}} [[Category:宮城県の神社]] [[Category:宮城県の旧村社]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:多賀城市の歴史]] [[Category:陸奥国|社0]]

1985年調査での推定樹齢約220年（江戸時代）、樹高16.8メートル、周囲2.2メートル。 * 陸奥総社宮の老杉（[[スギ]]） - 1985年調査での推定樹齢約600年（室町時代）、樹高25.6メートル、周囲4.88メートル。神社の神木で、正月に[[注連縄|しめ縄]]をかける。 File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|本殿 File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|ハクモクレン File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|スギ == 祭事 == 陸奥総社宮で年間に行われる祭事は次の通り[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html 祭神のご案内]（公式サイト）。。 * 初詣・元旦祭 （1月1日-3日） * どんと祭 （1月14日） * 節分祭 （2月第1土曜・日曜、第2土曜・日曜） * 例大祭 （4月第3日曜） - 神輿渡御。 * 七五三祭 （10月下旬-11月中） == 現地情報 == '''所在地''' * 宮城県多賀城市市川字奏社1 '''交通アクセス''' * [[東日本旅客鉄道]]（JR東日本）[[東北本線]] [[国府多賀城駅]] （徒歩30分） == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == * 多賀城市史編纂委員会 編 『多賀城市史』第1巻（原始・古代・中世）、多賀城市、1997年。 * 宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年10月 * {{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=|year=1987|chapter=市川村|title=[[日本歴史地名大系]] 4 宮城県の地名|publisher=[[平凡社]]|isbn=4582490042|ref={{Harvid|市川村（平凡社）|1987年}}}} * {{Cite book|和書|editor=中世諸国一宮制研究会編|author=|year=2000|chapter=|title=中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究|publisher=岩田書院|isbn=978-4872941708|ref={{Harvid|中世諸国一宮制|2000年}}}} == 外部リンク == {{Commonscat|Mutsusoushanomiya}} * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ 陸奥総社宮] - 1985年調査での推定樹齢約220年（江戸時代）、樹高16.8メートル、周囲2.2メートル。 * 陸奥総社宮の老杉（[[スギ]]） - 1985年調査での推定樹齢約600年（室町時代）、樹高25.6メートル、周囲4.88メートル。神社の神木で、正月に[[注連縄|しめ縄]]をかける。 File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|本殿 File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|ハクモクレン File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|スギ == 祭事 == 陸奥総社宮で年間に行われる祭事は次の通り[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html 祭神のご案内]（公式サイト）。。 * 初詣・元旦祭 （1月1日-3日） * どんと祭 （1月14日） * 節分祭 （2月第1土曜・日曜、第2土曜・日曜） * 例大祭 （4月第3日曜） - 神輿渡御。 * 七五三祭 （10月下旬-11月中） == 現地情報 == '''所在地''' * 宮城県多賀城市市川字奏社1 '''交通アクセス''' * [[東日本旅客鉄道]]（JR東日本）[[東北本線]] [[国府多賀城駅]] （徒歩30分） == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == * 多賀城市史編纂委員会 編 『多賀城市史』第1巻（原始・古代・中世）、多賀城市、1997年。 * 宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年10月 * {{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=|year=1987|chapter=市川村|title=[[日本歴史地名大系]] 4 宮城県の地名|publisher=[[平凡社]]|isbn=4582490042|ref={{Harvid|市川村（平凡社）|1987年}}}} * {{Cite book|和書|editor=中世諸国一宮制研究会編|author=|year=2000|chapter=|title=中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究|publisher=岩田書院|isbn=978-4872941708|ref={{Harvid|中世諸国一宮制|2000年}}}} == 関連項目 == * [[多賀城]] == 外部リンク == {{Commonscat|Mutsusoushanomiya}} * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ 陸奥総社宮] - 旧[[村社]] |創建 = 不詳 |本殿 = [[流造]] |別名 = 奏社宮 |札所等 = |例祭 = 4月第3日曜 |神事 = |地図 = {{Location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=陸奥総社宮|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|鳥居}}]] '''陸奥総社宮'''（むつそうしゃのみや/むつそうじゃぐう）は、[[宮城県]][[多賀城市]]市川にある[[神社]]。[[陸奥国]][[総社]]で、[[近代社格制度|旧社格]]は[[村社]]。 == 祭神 == 主祭神は次の2柱[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 陸奥総社宮]（宮城県神社庁）。。 * 八塩道老翁神 * 八塩道老女神 また、陸奥国内31[[郡]]の[[式内社]]100社の神霊を合わせ祀る。 == 歴史 == [[古代]]、[[国司]]には各国内の神社を巡拝する任務があった。これを効率化するため、各国の[[国府]]近くに国内の神を合祀した[[総社]]を設け、まとめて祭祀を行うようになった。この制は平安時代に広まったものであるが、陸奥国の総社について当時の記録はない。陸奥国府（[[多賀城]]）の近く、「奏社宮」と呼ばれていた当社を総社に比定する説が江戸時代から有力視されているが、当社で伝える古記録は失われており明らかでない{{Sfn|中世諸国一宮制|2000年|p=310}}。なお、[[鹽竈神社]]を総社とする説があるほか『多賀城市史』第1巻458頁。{{Sfn|中世諸国一宮制|2000年|p=310}}、『[[延喜式]]』[[延喜式神名帳|神名帳]]に載る「多賀神社」を当社に比定する説もある{{Sfn|中世諸国一宮制|2000年|p=310}}。 [[鎌倉時代]]には、陸奥留守職に任じられて「留守」姓を名乗るようになった伊沢氏により崇敬を受け、祭祀料として3,000刈の社地が寄進されたという。[[江戸時代]]になると[[仙台藩]]初代藩主の[[伊達政宗]]による領内寺社整備が行われ、[[法蓮寺 (塩竈市)|法蓮寺]]（[[鹽竈神社]][[別当]]）末寺の市川山神奏院が別当として置かれ社務が行われた。『宮城県神社名鑑』宮城県神社庁編 『宮城県神社名鑑』 宮城県神社庁、1976年1月。によれば、奏社宮には歴代藩主の尊崇が篤く、親拝代参などがあったという。 [[明治維新]]後、[[明治]]4年（[[1871年]]）10月に[[近代社格制度]]において[[村社]]に列した。明治41年（[[1908年]]）に貴船神社など7社が合祀されたほか、[[大正]]12年（[[1923年]]）8月には[[近代社格制度#諸社|神饌幣帛料供進神社]]に指定された[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html 陸奥総社宮について]（公式サイト）。。 現在も安産守護・海上守護・歳徳・武徳・大難除けの神として崇敬されている。 == 境内 == 社殿は本殿・拝殿からなる。 境内には多賀城市の保存樹木が2本ある『多賀城市史』第1巻27頁。以下の樹齢等の数値も同じ。。 * 陸奥総社宮の白木蓮（[[ハクモクレン]]） - 1985年調査での推定樹齢約220年（江戸時代）、樹高16.8メートル、周囲2.2メートル。 * 陸奥総社宮の老杉（[[スギ]]） - 1985年調査での推定樹齢約600年（室町時代）、樹高25.6メートル、周囲4.88メートル。神社の神木で、正月に[[注連縄|しめ縄]]をかける。 File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|本殿 File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|ハクモクレン File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|スギ == 祭事 == 陸奥総社宮で年間に行われる祭事は次の通り[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html 祭神のご案内]（公式サイト）。。 * 初詣・元旦祭 （1月1日-3日） * どんと祭 （1月14日） * 節分祭 （2月第1土曜・日曜、第2土曜・日曜） * 例大祭 （4月第3日曜） - 神輿渡御。 * 七五三祭 （10月下旬-11月中） == 現地情報 == '''所在地''' * 宮城県多賀城市市川字奏社1 '''交通アクセス''' * [[東日本旅客鉄道]]（JR東日本）[[東北本線]] [[国府多賀城駅]] （徒歩30分） == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == * 多賀城市史編纂委員会 編 『多賀城市史』第1巻（原始・古代・中世）、多賀城市、1997年。 * 宮城県神社庁 編　『宮城県神社名鑑』　宮城県神社庁　1976年10月 * {{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=|year=1987|chapter=市川村|title=[[日本歴史地名大系]] 4 宮城県の地名|publisher=[[平凡社]]|isbn=4582490042|ref={{Harvid|市川村（平凡社）|1987年}}}} * {{Cite book|和書|editor=中世諸国一宮制研究会編|author=|year=2000|chapter=|title=中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究|publisher=岩田書院|isbn=978-4872941708|ref={{Harvid|中世諸国一宮制|2000年}}}} == 関連項目 == * [[多賀城]] == 外部リンク == {{Commonscat|Mutsusoushanomiya}} * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ 陸奥総社宮] - {{Shrine | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deities = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{Location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * **White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')** – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * **Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')** – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|Main Hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == Festivals == Annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html Festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * **New Year's Festival** (January 1–3) * **Donto Festival** (January 14) * **Setsubun Festival** (First and second weekends of February) * **Annual Grand Festival** (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * **Shichi-Go-San Festival** (Late October–November) == Location and Access == '''Address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] [[Tohoku Main Line]] [[Kokufu-Tagajō Station]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ Official Website of Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] * [http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association) {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Miyagi Prefecture]] [[Category:Historical sites in Tagajō]] [[Category:Village shrines]] [[Category:Mutsu Province shrines]] [[Category:Sacred sites in Miyagi Prefecture]] [[Category:Tagajō City]]

As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * **White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')** – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * **Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')** – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * **New Year's festival** (January 1–3) * **Donto festival** (January 14) * **Setsubun festival** (First and second weekends of February) * **annual Grand festival** (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * **Shichi-Go-San festival** (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] [[Tohoku Main Line]] [[Kokufu-Tagajō Station]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ Official Website of Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] * [http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association) {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Miyagi Prefecture]] [[Category:Historical sites in Tagajō]] [[Category:Village shrines]] [[Category:Mutsu Province shrines]] [[Category:Sacred sites in Miyagi Prefecture]] [[Category:Tagajō City]] [[Category:original pages]] [[Category:original pages]][[Category:original pages]][[Category:original pages]]

As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * **White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')** – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * **Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')** – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * **White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')** – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * **Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')** – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * **New Year's festival** (January 1–3) * **Donto festival** (January 14) * **Setsubun festival** (First and second weekends of February) * **annual Grand festival** (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * **Shichi-Go-San festival** (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] [[Tohoku Main Line]] [[Kokufu-Tagajō Station]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ Official Website of Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] * [http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * **White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')** – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * **Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')** – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * **New Year's festival** (January 1–3) * **Donto festival** (January 14) * **Setsubun festival** (First and second weekends of February) * **annual Grand festival** (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * **Shichi-Go-San festival** (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] [[Tohoku Main Line]] [[Kokufu-Tagajō Station]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ Official Website of Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] * {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * **White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')** – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * **Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')** – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * **New Year's festival** (January 1–3) * **Donto festival** (January 14) * **Setsubun festival** (First and second weekends of February) * **annual Grand festival** (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * **Shichi-Go-San festival** (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * **White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')** – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * **Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')** – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * **New Year's festival** (January 1–3) * **Donto festival** (January 14) * **Setsubun festival** (First and second weekends of February) * **annual Grand festival** (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * **Shichi-Go-San festival** (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] [[Tohoku Main Line]] [[Kokufu-Tagajō Station]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ Official Website of Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] * As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] [[Tohoku Main Line]] [[Kokufu-Tagajō Station]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ Official Website of Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] * {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]]
