{{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mutsu Sōsha Shrine | image = [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya haiden.JPG|280px|Mutsu Sōsha Shrine]]
Worship Hall | address = Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|38|18|39.82|N|140|59|35.95|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine}} | deity = Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami
Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami | shrine rank = [[Mutsu Province|Provincial Shrine]]
Former [[Village Shrine]] | established = Unknown | main hall = [[Nagare-zukuri]] style | aliases = Sōsha Shrine | festivals = 3rd Sunday of April | map = {{location map|Japan Miyagi Prefecture|label=Mutsu Sōsha Shrine|float=center|relief=1|width=256}} }} [[File:Mutsu-soushanomiya torii.JPG|220px|right|thumb|{{center|Torii Gate}}]] '''Mutsu Sōsha Shrine''' ({{nihongo|陸奥総社宮|むつそうしゃのみや}}) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] [[Tohoku Main Line]] [[Kokufu-Tagajō Station]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ Official Website of Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] * [http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association) {{Shinto-stub}} {{Sōja shrines}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Mutsu Sōsha-no-miya]] [[Category:Completion tier 5]] [[Category: tier 5]] [[Category:11]] [[Category: Completion tier 5]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Miyagi Prefecture]] [[Category:Historical sites in Tagajō]] [[Category:Village shrines]] [[Category:Mutsu Province shrines]] [[Category:Sacred sites in Miyagi Prefecture]] [[Category:Tagajō City]] [[Category:1 revision imported]] [[Category:refreshing imported pages]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:New]] }} [[sn:Mutsu Sōsha-no-miya]] [[sn:utsu Sōsha-no-miya]] [[ja:陸奥総社宮]] {{DEFAULTSORT:Mutsu Sōsha-no-miya}}

As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[Edo period]], the [[Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|main hall File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|White Magnolia File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|Sacred Japanese Cedar == festivals == annual festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine include:[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html festivals at Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). * '''New Year's festival''' (January 1–3) * '''Donto festival''' (January 14) * '''Setsubun festival''' (First and second weekends of February) * '''annual Grand festival''' (3rd Sunday of April) – Features a portable shrine procession. * '''Shichi-Go-San festival''' (Late October–November) == location and Access == '''address''': Kanedate 1, Ichikawa Aza Sōsha, Tagajō City, Miyagi Prefecture, Japan '''Access''': * By Train: About a 30-minute walk from [[JR East]] [[Tohoku Main Line]] [[Kokufu-Tagajō Station]]. == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [http://sousyanomiya.jp/ Official Website of Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] * [http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association) {{Shinto-stub}} {{draft categories| }} {{Sōja shrines}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Mutsu Sōsha-no-miya]] [[Category:Completion tier 5]] [[Category:11]] [[Category: Completion tier 5]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Miyagi Prefecture]] [[Category:Historical sites in Tagajō]] [[Category:Village shrines]] [[Category:Mutsu Province shrines]] [[Category:Sacred sites in Miyagi Prefecture]] [[Category:Tagajō City]] [[Category:New]] }} [[sn:Mutsu Sōsha-no-miya]] [[sn:utsu Sōsha-no-miya]] [[ja:陸奥総社宮]] {{DEFAULTSORT:Mutsu Sōsha-no-miya}}

1985年調査での推定樹齢約220年（江戸時代）、樹高16.8メートル、周囲2.2メートル。 * 陸奥総社宮の老杉（[[スギ]]） - 1985年調査での推定樹齢約600年（室町時代）、樹高25.6メートル、周囲4.88メートル。神社の神木で、正月に[[注連縄|しめ縄]]をかける。 File:Mutsu-soushanomiya honden.JPG|本殿 File:Mutsu-soushanomiya hakumokuren.JPG|ハクモクレン File:Mutsu-soushanomiya sugi.JPG|スギ == 祭事 == 陸奥総社宮で年間に行われる祭事は次の通り[http://sousyanomiya.jp/schedule/index.html 祭神のご案内]（公式サイト）。。 * 初詣・元旦祭 （1月1日-3日） * どんと祭 （1月14日） * 節分祭 （2月第1土曜・日曜、第2土曜・日曜） * 例大祭 （4月第3日曜） - As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. To streamline this responsibility, provincial shrines were established near the provincial capitals to enshrine the region's deities collectively. While this practice became common during the Heian period, there are no direct historical records regarding Mutsu's provincial shrine. The shrine now known as Mutsu Sōsha is widely believed to have served this purpose, a theory supported by its historical name, "Sōsha Shrine," and its location near the former [[:en:Tagajō|Tagajō]] provincial capital.{{Cite book|editor=Medieval Provincial Shrine Study Group|year=2000|title=Basic Studies on the Medieval Provincial Shrine System|publisher=Iwata Shoin|isbn=978-4872941708}} During the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], the shrine received patronage from the Izawa clan, who held the title of "keepers of Mutsu" (''Mutsu no Rusushoku''). They reportedly donated 3,000 ''kari'' of land for shrine upkeep.[http://sousyanomiya.jp/history/index.html About Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Official Website). In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the [[:en:Date clan|Date clan]], rulers of the [[Sendai Domain]], conducted significant renovations and established the nearby Ichikawa-zan Shinsoin Temple as the shrine's custodian. In the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was classified as a [[Village Shrine]] under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system in 1871. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters. The cedar is a sacred tree adorned with ''shimenawa'' during the New Year. As the provincial shrine (''sōsha'') of the former [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], it serves as a collective enshrinement of the deities of the region's shrines. == Deities == The shrine enshrines the following primary deities:[http://miyagi-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja-search/detail.php?sortmode=&chinzachi=%E5%A4%9A%E8%B3%80%E5%9F%8E%E5%B8%82&jinja_name=&jinja_kana=&jinja_sort_key=t_shrine.kana%2C+t_shrine.address&jinja_sortdesc=&per_page_def=15&page_jinja=0&jinja_cnt=6&code=310020331&PC=1 Mutsu Sōsha Shrine] (Miyagi Prefecture Shrine Association). * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Kami (八塩道老翁神) * Yatsushio Michi no Oji-no-Megami (八塩道老女神) Additionally, the shrine collectively enshrines the spirits of 100 shrines from the 31 districts of Mutsu Province. == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors (''kokushi'') were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdictions. In 1908, several smaller shrines, including Kibune Shrine, were merged into Mutsu Sōsha Shrine. It was designated as a shrine receiving imperial offerings in 1923. Today, the shrine remains a site of devotion for safe childbirth, maritime safety, protection from misfortune, and other blessings. == Shrine Grounds == The shrine complex consists of a main hall (''honden'') and a worship hall (''haiden''). Notable trees on the shrine grounds include:Tagajō City Historical Commission, ''Tagajō City History,'' Vol. 1, 1997. * '''White Magnolia (''Hakumokuren'')''' – Estimated to be approximately 220 years old (planted during the Edo period), standing 16.8 meters tall with a circumference of 2.2 meters. * '''Japanese Cedar (''Sugi'')''' – Estimated to be around 600 years old (dating to the Muromachi period), standing 25.6 meters tall with a circumference of 4.88 meters.
